```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Household surveys often ask some questions only of people who pass a filter
question: advice about blood pressure only of people already diagnosed,
questions about a child only of recent mothers, questions about a service only
of its users. If such items enter a multiple correspondence analysis (MCA)
index, the coding of the skip decides how much of the filter enters the index,
and the filter can take the index over. This vignette runs the audit on a
simulated survey and shows what happens to targeting.

## A survey with filtered items

`simulate_filtered_survey()` draws six three-level deprivation items, a latent
need, contact with care that depends on cluster access more than on need, and
four advice items asked only of people in contact with care.

```{r}
library(skipMCA)
dev <- simulate_filtered_survey(n_clusters = 200, contact = 0.5, seed = 1)
items <- paste0("advice", 1:4)
inputs <- paste0("x", 1:6)
table(asked = !is.na(dev$advice1))
```

## The audit

`skip_audit()` needs development data only. It reports, for each coding, the
mean squared correlation ratio of the filtered items with eligibility (how much
of the filter each item carries, which the closed form gives exactly), the
inertia ratio (the filtered block's maximum axial inertia times its number of
items, against the substantive block's), and how much of the index's first axis
the filtered block and eligibility explain.

```{r}
audit <- skip_audit(dev, items, inputs, budget = 0.1)
audit
```

Missing single, the skip as its own category, gives every filtered item a
squared correlation ratio with eligibility of 1, and the first axis is the
filter. Subset MCA keeps one minus the share
asked. Missing fuzzy average, which gives the skipped the answers of those
asked, carries none. Under it, a filtered item's squared correlation ratio with
any score is at most the share asked, so its capture ratio stays low.

```{r}
audit$items[audit$items$item == "advice1", ]
```

## What capture does to targeting

Fit the index under two codings, deploy it in a population where only 20
percent have been in contact with care, and compare the allocations against
the true need.

```{r}
target <- simulate_filtered_survey(n_clusters = 200, contact = 0.2, seed = 2)
score_with <- function(coding) {
  fit <- skip_mca(dev, items, inputs, coding = coding, orient = dev$need)
  predict(fit, target)[, 1]
}
codings <- c("category", "subset", "no", "fuzzy_average", "drop")
round(sapply(codings, function(cd)
  targeting_metrics(score_with(cd), target$need, target$cluster)), 3)
```

The index that codes the skip as its own category ranks communities by their
contact with care, which here is nearly unrelated to need. Subset MCA and the
"no" coding, just above an inertia ratio of 1 in the audit, lose part of the
ranking. Missing fuzzy average ranks communities as well as dropping the
items, because the filter has no direction in it to follow.

## When a dominant filter is benign

The audit cannot decide one thing: whether passing the filter is part of what
the index should measure. Owning land is part of wealth, so a block of
land-use items asked only of landowners may rightly pull a wealth index. Contact
with care is not part of need, so a need index should not follow it. When the
filter measures access, use missing fuzzy average or drop the filtered items,
and judge the index by its allocation over everyone it will serve.
